title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
authors: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun

pages.title: The core idea
pages.subtitle: Make very deep networks easy to train

blocks.html: The question this page answers: why did making a neural network deeper — which should only add capacity — suddenly start making it worse, and how does one trick fix it? By 2015, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia (Kaiming He and colleagues) had hit a wall. Adding more layers to a convolutional network past a couple of dozen made accuracy drop, and not because of overfitting: the training error itself got worse. That should be impossible in theory.

A concrete way to see the paradox. Suppose a 20-layer network already works well. Now build a 56-layer network. In principle the deep one could copy the 20-layer network exactly in its first 20 layers and make the remaining 36 layers do nothing — just pass their input straight through (the identity mapping). That construction guarantees the 56-layer net is at least as good as the 20-layer one. Yet in practice gradient descent could not find that solution: the 56-layer plain net had higher training error. So the bottleneck was not the model's capacity — it was the optimization. Plain stacks of layers are simply hard for SGD to fit once they get deep.

The fix — residual learning. Instead of asking a few stacked layers to learn the full desired mapping $H(x)$ directly, ask them to learn only the difference from the input, the residual $F(x) = H(x) - x$, and then add the input back so the block outputs $F(x) + x$. If the best thing a block can do is nothing (the identity), the layers only have to push their weights toward zero — trivial — rather than laboriously learning an identity through nonlinear layers.
We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions.

The numbers. With this one change the authors trained networks of unprecedented depth. A 152-layer ResNet — 8× deeper than VGG-19 — won the ILSVRC 2015 ImageNet classification challenge, and an ensemble reached 3.57% top-5 error, while still having lower computational complexity (FLOPs) than VGG. The same residual building block also won the ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation tracks that year — a clean sweep that proved it was a general-purpose tool, not an ImageNet-specific trick.

Why it still matters. The skip connection introduced here is now nearly universal: it is the reason Transformers, DenseNets, U-Nets, and almost every modern deep architecture can stack dozens or hundreds of layers without collapsing. ResNet turned depth from a liability into a resource.

The intuition first. The deep learning revolution of 2012–2014 had a clear theme: depth helps. AlexNet (8 layers) beat shallow methods; VGG (16–19 layers) and GoogLeNet (22 layers) pushed further. The natural extrapolation was ‘just keep stacking.’ But there was a hidden ceiling, and this paper is about smashing through it.

The surprising observation. As plain networks got deeper, accuracy first saturated and then degraded rapidly. The authors stress that this is not caused by overfitting, because overfitting would lower training error while raising test error. Here the training error itself rises. Their headline example: on CIFAR-10, a 56-layer plain network had higher training error than a 20-layer plain network (their Figure 1), and the same effect appeared on ImageNet with 18 vs 34 layers.

rows: not overfitting: train error went UP

blocks.html: What this tells us. The issue is not capacity — the deeper net contains the shallower one as a special case — it is trainability. Deep stacks of nonlinear layers struggle to approximate even the identity mapping, so the solver cannot reach a solution at least as good as the shallow network nested inside it. The authors are careful to note this is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients alone, since these networks already used normalized initialization and Batch Normalization, which keep early-layer gradients healthy; something about the optimization landscape of very deep plain nets is intrinsically hard.

A concrete picture. Imagine the optimal job for some block is ‘leave the features alone.’ For a plain block to do that, several convolution + ReLU layers must conspire to compute an exact identity — a precise nonlinear arrangement that SGD rarely stumbles onto. For a residual block, ‘leave it alone’ just means $F(x) \approx 0$, i.e. drive the weights toward zero. Zero is the most comfortable place a weight matrix can sit (it is where weight decay already pulls it). Residual connections hand the optimizer an easy default to fall back on, so adding a layer can never hurt much — in the worst case it learns to do nothing.

Trivia. The degradation problem had been observed by others, but ResNet was the first to give a clean, scalable remedy. The idea of skip connections itself echoes earlier work (Highway Networks, LSTM gating), but ResNet's choice of a parameter-free identity shortcut — rather than a learned gate — is what made it cheap enough to scale to hundreds of layers.

pages.title: The residual block
pages.subtitle: A shortcut that adds the input back

blocks.html: The building block. Take an input $x$, run it through a couple of weight layers to produce a residual $F(x)$, then add the untouched input back through a shortcut (skip) connection. Concretely the block computes:

Reading it term by term. $y$ is the block’s output (a tensor of the same shape as $x$). $x$ is the block’s input. $F(x, \{W_i\})$ is the residual function learned by the stacked weight layers, with $\{W_i\}$ their weights. For a typical two-layer block, $F = W_2\,\sigma(W_1 x)$, where $W_1, W_2$ are convolution weights and $\sigma$ is the ReLU nonlinearity $\max(0,\cdot)$. The $+\,x$ term is the identity shortcut: it carries the input forward unchanged and adds it element-wise to $F$. Crucially the shortcut has no parameters and almost no extra compute, so a residual net costs essentially the same as its plain twin — making the plain-vs-residual comparison perfectly fair.

When the shapes do not match. If $F(x)$ and $x$ have different dimensions — which happens when a block changes the number of channels or downsamples spatially — the plain addition is undefined. The fix is a linear projection $W_s$ on the shortcut so the dimensions line up:

Reading it. $W_s$ is a learned matrix (implemented as a $1\times1$ convolution with the right stride) that maps $x$ into the same shape as $F(x)$ before the sum. The authors found this is only needed for matching dimensions; using projections on every shortcut gives marginally better accuracy but costs more, so identity shortcuts are the default and projections are reserved for the few dimension-changing blocks.

The order of operations. Each weight layer is followed by Batch Normalization, the element-wise sum happens after the second BN, and a final ReLU is applied after the addition. So the structure is: conv → BN → ReLU → conv → BN → (add shortcut) → ReLU.

blocks.text: Why this fixes the gradient flow

blocks.html: The deep reason it works. Because the output is $F(x)+x$, the gradient of the loss with respect to $x$ contains a term that flows straight through the identity branch — the derivative of $+x$ is just 1. So even if the gradient through the weight layers $F$ becomes tiny, a clean copy of the gradient still reaches earlier layers undiminished. This additive ‘gradient highway’ is exactly why stacking 100+ residual blocks stays trainable while the equivalent plain stack does not.

Design rationale & alternatives. One could imagine making the shortcut a learned gate (as in Highway Networks, where a gate decides how much of $x$ to pass). ResNet deliberately keeps it a plain identity: a gate adds parameters, can saturate, and can choke the gradient highway when closed. The parameter-free identity is simpler, never blocks the gradient, and scales to extreme depth — a recurring lesson that the simplest version of an idea is often the one that scales.

pages.title: Going very deep: the bottleneck
pages.subtitle: 1x1 convolutions to stay cheap at 50+ layers

blocks.html: The problem at 50+ layers. The basic two-$3\times3$-conv block is fine up to 34 layers, but stacking many of them at full channel width (256, 512, …) is expensive: a $3\times3$ convolution’s cost grows with the square of the channel count. To reach 50, 101, and 152 layers within a sane compute budget, the authors redesigned the block as a bottleneck.

The analogy. Think of squeezing the data through a narrow neck before doing the expensive work, then expanding it back. Three convolutions do this: a cheap $1\times1$ conv shrinks the channels, the costly $3\times3$ conv does its spatial work on the now-thin tensor, and a final $1\times1$ conv restores the width so the shortcut sum lines up.

items: $1\times1$ conv: squeeze channels (e.g. 256 → 64), so the expensive $3\times3$ runs on a thin tensor.
$3\times3$ conv: the actual feature extraction, now cheap because it operates on 64 channels instead of 256.
$1\times1$ conv: expand back (64 → 256) so the output matches the shortcut for the element-wise add.

blocks.html: Why the identity shortcut matters even more here. The bottleneck’s two ends are high-dimensional (256 channels). If the shortcut had to be a learned projection, it would connect those two fat ends and roughly double the block’s parameters and FLOPs. Keeping the shortcut a parameter-free identity is precisely what makes the deep bottleneck models efficient — a 152-layer ResNet (11.3 billion FLOPs) is still cheaper than VGG-16/19 (~15–20 billion FLOPs).

rows: ILSVRC’15 winner, lower FLOPs than VGG

blocks.html: Trivia. The architecture follows two simple design rules borrowed from VGG: layers with the same output feature-map size have the same number of filters, and whenever the spatial size is halved the number of filters is doubled (so the per-layer compute stays roughly constant). Downsampling is done with stride-2 convolutions rather than pooling, and the network ends in a single global-average-pooling layer plus one fully-connected classifier — far fewer FC parameters than VGG’s heavy classifier head.

The decisive comparison. On ImageNet the authors trained matched plain and residual nets at 18 and 34 layers. The result is a clean controlled experiment: a plain 34-layer net does worse than a plain 18-layer net (the degradation problem in action), but the residual 34-layer net beats the residual 18-layer net and also converges faster. The only difference between each plain/residual pair is the skip connections — same depth, same FLOPs — so the gain is attributable to residual learning alone.

Pushing to the extreme. Going deeper kept helping. ResNet-152 had the lowest single-model error, and the winning ensemble reached 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set — first place in ILSVRC 2015, roughly halving the previous year’s best. For perspective, that is at or below the often-cited ~5% human top-5 error on ImageNet.

Why this was a big deal. Before ResNet, the field genuinely did not know whether networks much deeper than ~30 layers were trainable at all. ResNet showed the answer was yes — the obstacle had been optimization, not principle — and it did so while being computationally lighter than the previous champion. Depth had become a knob you could simply turn up.

The optimization stress test (CIFAR-10). To probe how far depth could go, the authors trained ResNets on the small CIFAR-10 dataset out to 110 layers and even 1202 layers. A 110-layer ResNet trains cleanly where a plain net of that depth fails outright. The 1202-layer net still optimizes fine (no degradation) though it slightly overfits this tiny dataset — which is itself the point: the failure mode is now overfitting (a capacity/regularization issue), not the optimization wall that stopped plain nets. This is direct evidence that residual learning solves an optimization problem.

Transfer to detection and segmentation. The same ResNet backbone, dropped into the Faster R-CNN detection pipeline in place of VGG-16, gave large gains essentially for free. The ResNet-based entry won the ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation challenges of 2015 — a near sweep with a single underlying idea.
Solely due to our extremely deep representations, we obtain a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset.

Why a better classifier backbone helps detection. Detectors like Faster R-CNN compute one shared convolutional feature map and reuse it for both region proposals and classification. A stronger, deeper backbone produces richer features, so everything downstream improves at once. This is exactly why ResNet-50/101 became the default feature extractor across computer vision for the rest of the decade.

The lasting legacy. ResNet did more than win a competition; it made depth a usable resource. The skip connection is now a near-universal component. It appears in DenseNets (which connect every layer to every later one), U-Nets (which skip encoder features to the decoder for segmentation), and — most consequentially — inside the Transformer, where every self-attention and feed-forward sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection for exactly the same reason ResNet introduced it: to let gradients flow through very deep stacks. The GPT and BERT families, and modern LLMs, are residual networks at heart.

items: Reframed the learning target as the residual $F(x)=H(x)-x$, making identity-like mappings trivial to learn (drive $F$ toward 0).
Identity shortcuts add no parameters and create a gradient highway that bypasses the nonlinear layers.
Bottleneck blocks ($1\times1$–$3\times3$–$1\times1$) keep 50/101/152-layer models cheap — ResNet-152 has fewer FLOPs than VGG.
Won ILSVRC 2015 at 3.57% top-5 error and swept the detection/segmentation tracks.
Became the standard backbone for detection, segmentation, and the residual idea underpins the Transformer era.

blocks.html: Common misconception. ResNet is sometimes described as ‘solving vanishing gradients.’ That is only part of the story — the networks already used Batch Normalization, so gradients were not literally vanishing. The deeper contribution is reshaping the optimization landscape so that deep stacks become easy to fit, with the identity as an effortless fallback. Kaiming He won the Marr Prize / best-paper recognition for this work, and it is among the most cited papers in all of computer science.
